Section III: Historical Case Studies
2008: Paulson’s “bazooka” rescued bondholders, not shareholders
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were taken over on 7 September, and the 10-year yield then fell together with the S&P 500
What happened
10-year Treasury yield, %
1 13 Jul: With Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac shares down about 75% in 2008, Paulson asks Congress for authority to backstop them.
2 30 Jul: The powers become law. His argument: if markets know you have a “bazooka”, you may never have to use it.
3 7 Sep: He uses it anyway: both firms are taken over, with up to $100bn each (about $190bn is eventually drawn).
Share prices, 31 Dec 2007 = 100
4 25 Nov: The Fed pledges to buy up to $600bn of agency debt and mortgage bonds. The 10-year falls 24bp that day.
S&P 500 Fannie Mae
What does this teach an equity analyst?
A backstop for debt is not a backstop for equity Mortgage rates fell 42bp in a week; the shares lost 90% and 83%.
Lower yields do not help stocks when fear drives them The 10-year fell 179bp in 2008, and the S&P 500 still lost 38.5%.

Section III: Historical Case Studies
2013 Taper Tantrum: talk lifted yields a full point, yet stocks rose 30%
The Fed changed nothing until December; the 10-year rose from 1.94% to 2.98% (21 May to 5 Sep), all of it in real yields
What happened
10-year Treasury yield, %
Nominal Real 1 2 3 4
1 22 May: Fed Chair Bernanke says the Fed could soon slow its $85bn-a-month bond buying. No rate hike, no change yet.
2 19 Jun: He sets a timetable to end purchases by mid-2014. The 10year rises 40bp in a week; the S&P 500 loses 3.9% in two days.
3 18 Sep: Markets expect the taper to start. The Fed holds off and the 10-year drops 17bp in a day.
S&P 500, index level
4 18 Dec: The taper arrives: purchases are cut to $75bn a month. The 10-year moves 4bp; the S&P 500 closes at a record.
What does this teach an equity analyst?
Markets price the expectation, not the event The 10-year rose 104bp on talk of tapering, and 4bp when it came.
Growth and a yield gap let stocks absorb the rise S&P 500 +29.6% with a 2.8-point yield gap; end-2025: 0.0

Key Takeaways
Key takeaways: four questions to ask when yields move
What an analyst should check when yields move, and what each episode in this deck taught us
Four questions to ask
What each episode taught us
1 Which block moved? The Fed path, inflation compensation or the term premium
1 1996 to 2000: valuation alone doesn’t time the top The Fed, then earnings, ended the run three years later
2 Are earnings rising with it? If yes, stocks can absorb it; if not, multiples compress
2 2008: a backstop for debt is not one for equity Mortgage rates fell 42bp; shareholders lost 90% in a day
3 How much yield gap is left? Earnings yield vs 10-year; premium vs 4.25% average
3 2013: growth-driven rises get absorbed The 10-year rose 126bp over 2013, yet the S&P 500 rose 29.6%
4 How long are the cash flows? Growth and long-duration sectors take the biggest hit
4 2026: a real-yield rise with no yield gap left Earnings must keep delivering for today’s 19.1x to hold
Our answer: yields hit stocks through the discount rate; whether a rise hurts depends on why yields move and if earnings keep up.
Ask why yields are moving before asking how far: the reason decides what happens to stocks
